The set $S = \left\{\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^n \mid n \in \mathbb{N}\right\}$ is **countable**, since it is indexed by $\mathbb{N}$.

**Proof.**

Recall that Lebesgue outer measure $\mu^*$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is defined for any $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ by

$$\mu^*(A) = \inf\left\{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \ell(I_k) : A \subseteq \bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} I_k,\; I_k \text{ intervals}\right\}.$$

A fundamental property of $\mu^*$ is **countable subadditivity**: for any countable collection of sets $\{A_k\}$,

$$\mu^*\!\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} A_k\right) \le \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \mu^*(A_k).$$

In particular, every singleton $\{x\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ has outer measure $0$, since for any $\varepsilon > 0$ the interval $(x - \varepsilon/2,\, x + \varepsilon/2)$ covers $\{x\}$ and has length $\varepsilon$, giving $\mu^*(\{x\}) \le \varepsilon$ for all $\varepsilon > 0$.

Since $S$ is countable, write $S = \{x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots\} = \bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} \{x_k\}$. By countable subadditivity,

$$\mu^*(S) \le \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \mu^*(\{x_k\}) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 0 = 0.$$

Since outer measure is non-negative, $\mu^*(S) \ge 0$. Therefore

$$\boxed{\mu^*(S) = 0.}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
thinking: The problem asks to compute the outer measure of the set $\{(1+1/n)^n \mid n \in \mathbb{N}\}$. This is a countable set, so its outer measure (Lebesgue outer measure) is 0.
